name: Cranioplasty for facial contouring

card.summary: Cranioplasty reconstructs or reshapes the skull with bone, cement or implants, restoring or changing head and forehead contour.
card.note: Neurosurgical operation; published complication rates are substantial and the literature is mostly about repairing defects.

quick.overview:
Cranioplasty is an operation that repairs or reshapes the skull by filling or covering a defect with the patient's own bone or with materials such as titanium, acrylic or hydroxyapatite. For appearance, the payoff is a restored or altered head contour, for instance removing a visible dent or sunken area, and in facial plastic surgery it is also used to change forehead and skull shape.

Most published research concerns repairing defects after trauma or decompressive surgery, where reviews describe it as restoring the natural cosmesis and protective barrier of the skull. Cosmetic skull contouring appears in looksmaxxing discussion as part of hardmaxxing, but its medical literature rests mainly on reconstructive patients.
quick.how: A surgeon opens the scalp, prepares the area, and fixes bone or implant material to the skull, commonly with titanium plates and screws. Material is chosen for the case: the patient's own bone, custom-fit synthetics or mesh. Imaging before and after surgery and antibiotic cover are standard in the reconstructive setting, and recovery is supervised by the surgical team.
quick.risks: Complication rates in the reconstructive literature range widely, with infection, bone resorption, wound problems, bleeding and fluid collections among those reported; children face higher bone resorption risk with their own bone. It is performed under general anaesthesia on the skull, so assessment and the choice of material are specialist decisions.

lead: Cranioplasty is the surgical repair or reshaping of the skull. A defect, whether from injury, a previous operation such as decompressive craniectomy, or a contour wish, is filled or covered with the patient's own bone, donor tissue or a synthetic material [15] [1][12].

Its appearance purpose is explicit in the medical literature. A neurosurgical review describes the operation as restoring natural cosmesis and the protective barrier of the skull [1], and Wikipedia lists the cosmetic aim as restoring normal skull shape and avoiding a sunken scalp. A facial plastic surgery review treats the procedure within the craniofacial specialty [12].
The topic is discussed in hardmaxxing circles as a route to altering forehead and skull contour. The published research is mainly reconstructive, covering materials, timing and complications.

chain: Filled or covered with bone, cement or implant
Smoother, restored or altered skull shape
angle.text: The implant or graft physically changes the skull's outline. In reconstructive use this removes depressions and restores a normal contour; cosmetic contouring applies the same materials to shape the forehead or vault.

paras: After an incision, the scalp and underlying muscle are lifted, the defect is cleaned and the implant is secured to the surrounding skull, often with titanium plates and screws [15]. Review articles cover patient selection, timing, materials, operative technique, postoperative care and complication management [1].

Autologous bone is regarded as a preferred option, particularly in children, but is prone to resorption [4]. Polymethyl methacrylate (acrylic cement) prostheses have been used in clinical series [6][7]. Titanium is associated with lower infection rates but costs more, and hydroxyapatite integrates well and suits cosmetic results, mainly in small defects [15]. A history of the field traces materials from antiquity to modern implants [5][11]. Porous tantalum has been studied as another biomaterial [13].

The reconstructive literature includes children and adults, with a dedicated review of paediatric cranioplasty noting that the approach has been refined from earlier extrapolation from adult care and must be tailored to each defect [3]. Craniosynostosis, early fusion of skull sutures that distorts head shape, is a separate condition treated by vault remodelling and related surgery [2].

A review of complications and a case analysis of 62 cranioplasties after decompressive craniectomy describe infection and other problems as common enough to require active management [9][10]. Infection rates in a systematic review depended on surgical timing, material and flap preservation [14]. Bone resorption after autologous cranioplasty is a recognised problem in children and adolescents [4]. Wikipedia [15] gives complication rates of about 15% to 41%, including infection, resorption, haematoma and seizures.

Human studies are case series and reviews of reconstructive cranioplasty. A 312-patient single-surgeon series with 449 procedures examined long-term outcomes by material [8], and trials and series of PMMA cranioplasty have been reported [6][7]. No studies were found of cranioplasty done purely for facial contouring in otherwise healthy patients.

timeline.event: Earliest known cranioplasty in pre-Columbian Peru [15].
Macewen's report helps popularise bone autografts [15].
Long-term outcome review of 312 patients published [8].
